etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English bodi, bodiȝ, from Old English bodiġ (“body, trunk, chest, torso, height, stature”), from Proto-West Germanic *bodag (“body, trunk”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewdʰ- (“to be awake, observe”). Cognate with Old High German botah (whence Swabian Bottich (“body, torso”)).

definitions.definition: The physical structure of a human or animal seen as one single organism. [from 9th c.]

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, 1 Corinthians 12:15–20:
quote.text: If the foot shall say, Because I am not the hand, I am not of the body: is it therefore not of the body?And if the eare shall say, Because I am not the eye, I am not of the body: is it therefore not of the body?If the whole body were an eye, where were the hearing? If the whole were hearing, where were the smelling?But now hath God set the members, euery one of them in the body, as it hath pleased him.And if they were all one member, where were the body?But now are they many members, yet but one body.

definitions.definition: The fleshly or corporeal nature of a human, as opposed to the spirit or soul. [from 13th c.]
A corpse. [from 13th c.]
(archaic or informal except in compounds) A person. [from 13th c.]

quote.text: Indeed, if it belonged to a poor body, it would be another thing; but so great a lady, to be sure, can never want it  […]

quote.citation: 1876, Mark Twain [pseudonym; Samuel Langhorne Clemens], chapter 28, in The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, Hartford, Conn.: The American Publishing Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: Sometime I've set right down and eat WITH him. But you needn't tell that. A body's got to do things when he's awful hungry he wouldn't want to do as a steady thing.

quote.citation: 1913, Joseph C[rosby] Lincoln, chapter V, in Mr. Pratt’s Patients, New York, N.Y., London: D[aniel] Appleton and Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: “Well,” I says, “I cal’late a body could get used to Tophet if he stayed there long enough.” ¶ She flared up; the least mite of a slam at Doctor Wool was enough to set her going.

definitions.definition: (sociology) A human being, regarded as marginalized or oppressed.

quote.citation: 1999, Devon Carbado, Black Men on Race, Gender, and Sexuality: A Critical Reader, page 87:
quote.text: This, of course, was not about the State, but it was certainly an invasion: black bodies acting out in a public domain circumscribed by a racist culture. The Garvey movement presents an example of black bodies transgressing racialized spatial boundaries.

quote.citation: 2012, Trystan T. Cotten, Transgender Migrations, page 3:
quote.text: In doing so, Haritaworn also rethinks the marginality of transgender bodies and practices in queer movements and spaces.

quote.citation: 2016, Laura Harrison, Brown Bodies, White Babies, page 5:
quote.text: As the title suggests, this project is particularly interested in how race intersects with reproductive technologies—how brown bodies are deployed in the creation of white babies.

definitions.definition: Physical frame.
The torso, the main structure of a human or animal frame excluding the extremities (limbs, head, tail). [from 9th c.]
The largest or most important part of anything, as distinct from its appendages or accessories. [from 11th c.]
(archaic) The section of a dress extending from the neck to the waist, excluding the arms. [from 16th c.]
The content of a letter, message, or other printed or electronic document, as distinct from signatures, salutations, headers, and so on. [from 17th c.]
(programming) The code of a subroutine, contrasted to its signature and parameters. [from 20th c.]
(architecture, of a church) nave.
Main section.
A group of people having a common purpose or opinion; a mass. [from 16th c.]
An organisation, company or other authoritative group. [from 17th c.]
A unified collection of details, knowledge or information. [from 17th c.]
Coherent group.
Any physical object or material thing. [from 14th c.]
(uncountable) Substance; physical presence. [from 17th c.]

quote.citation: 1922 October 26, Virginia Woolf, chapter 1, in Jacob’s Room, Richmond, London:  […]  Leonard & Virginia Woolf at the Hogarth Press, →OCLC; republished London: The Hogarth Press, 1960, →OCLC:
quote.text: The voice had an extraordinary sadness. Pure from all body, pure from all passion, going out into the world, solitary, unanswered, breaking against rocks—so it sounded.

definitions.definition: (uncountable) Comparative viscosity, solidity or substance (in wine, colours etc.). [from 17th c.]

quote.citation: 1989 August 12, Caroline Foty, “Hindsights”, in Gay Community News, volume 17, number 5, page 7:
quote.text: "I’d Be Lost Without You" seems somewhat out of place from a vocal viewpoint — Lewis’s slightly reedy middle soprano is very expressive and absolutely true, but doesn’t have enough dark body to fully deal with the torchy melody.

definitions.definition: An agglomeration of some substance, especially one that would be otherwise uncountable.

quote.citation: 1806 June 26, Thomas Paine, “The cause of Yellow Fever and the means of preventing it, in places not yet infected with it, addressed to the Board of Health in America”, in The political and miscellaneous works of Thomas Paine, page 179:
quote.text: In a gentle breeze, the whole body of air, as far as the breeze extends, moves at the rate of seven or eight miles an hour; in a high wind, at the rate of seventy, eighty, or an hundred miles an hour  […]

quote.citation: 2012 March 19, Helge Løseth, Nuno Rodrigues, Peter R. Cobbold, “World's largest extrusive body of sand?”, in Geology, volume 40, number 5:
quote.text: Using three-dimensional seismic and well data from the northern North Sea, we describe a large (10 km3) body of sand and interpret it as extrusive.

quote.citation: 2018, VOA Learning English > China's Melting Glacier Brings Visitors, Adds to Climate Concerns‎[1]:
quote.text: The huge body of ice is in the southeastern edge of a Central Asian region called the Third Pole.

definitions.definition: Material entity.
(printing) The shank of a type, or the depth of the shank (by which the size is indicated).

quote.citation: 1992, Mary Kay Duggan, Italian Music Incunabula: Printers and Type, page 99:
quote.text: The stemless notes could have been cast on a body as short as 4 mm but were probably cast on bodies of the standard 14 mm size for ease of composition.

definitions.definition: (geometry) A three-dimensional object, such as a cube or cone.
(transitive, often with forth) To give body or shape to something.

quote.citation: c. 1595–1596 (date written), William Shakespeare, “A Midsommer Nights Dreame”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies: Published According to the True Originall Copies (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, (please specify the act number in uppercase Roman numerals, and the scene number in lowercase Roman numerals):
quote.text: And as imagination bodies forth / The forms of things unknown, the poet’s pen / Turns them to shapes and gives to airy nothing / A local habitation and a name.

quote.citation: 1851 March 22, “The Foreign Country at Home. IV. Abergavenny to Swansea.”, in Leigh Hunt, editor, Leigh Hunt’s Journal; a Miscellany for the Cultivation of the Memorable, the Progressive, and the Beautiful, volume I, number 16, London:  […]  Stewart & Murray, […], →OCLC, page 255:
quote.text: [A]s you stand on the steps of the Castle Green in this strange place, you feel quite floaty. This you are told is the scene of the Merthyr riots; and you feel still floatier as you body forth before your eyes a picture like the following—  […]

quote.citation: 1981, William Irwin Thompson, The Time Falling Bodies Take to Light: Mythology, Sexuality and the Origins of Culture, London: Rider/Hutchinson & Co., page 175:
quote.text: The drama of the storehouse on earth has its counterpart in Heaven, and if we accept the insights of both Jacobsen and von Dechend, we can see that the myth is bodying forth a principle which will later be expressed in the Hermetic axiom, “As above, so below.” In fact, it is precisely this relationship between above and below that the myth explores.

definitions.definition: To construct the bodywork of a car.
(transitive) To embody.

quote.text: I don’t say, one bodies the other / One’s spiritual truth; / But I do say it’s hard to lose either, / When you have both.

definitions.definition: (by extension) To utterly defeat someone.

quote.text: I keep getting bodied by kids half my age.

definitions.definition: (transitive, slang, African-American Vernacular) To murder someone.
